tool.name: The Divine Council Index
tool.heroSubtitle: Passages where the unseen realm is acting, grouped by thread.

link.empty: No post on this passage yet.

footer.text: The method. Nothing here is offered as the settled answer. Each passage has a problem in it, and every entry names that problem first. The claim is narrower than certainty and harder to dismiss: this reading resolves more of the problems at once, across more passages, with fewer separate patches than the alternatives. That is coverage, not proof. So every entry also carries what this reading still fails to explain, and what the competing readings leave sitting.

footer.text: How to read the grades. Explicit means the text says it. Implied means the text assumes it. Contested means the reading rests on a decision that can be argued the other way, and several of the load-bearing passages here are filed contested on purpose.

entries.title: Genesis 1:26-27
entries.summary: Let us make man in our image, and then a singular verb does the making.
entries.plain: The real question: why does God say “let us make” and then act alone in the very next line? The candidates are multiple gods, the Trinity, or something else. **Let's build a shed. I built a shed.** The first sentence includes other people. The second one says who actually swung the hammer. Both can be true about the same shed, and nobody thinks the second sentence contradicts the first. This card reads it as an announcement to a real council, not a description of who did the work.
entries.prob: God speaks in the plural and then acts in the singular, one verse apart. Any reading has to account for both halves, and most accounts only handle one.
entries.res: Read as an announcement to the council rather than a description of who does the work, both halves stand. Verse 26 addresses a room. Verse 27 records a single actor.
entries.cost: It does not tell us who else was in the room or what they contributed, and the honest answer is that the text does not say.
entries.alt: The plural of majesty explanation has trouble with the verb form. The Trinity reading may be true theologically and still does not describe what a first hearer would have understood. Both leave the singular-plural seam unexplained rather than resolved.
entries.not: **Not multiple creators.** The singular verb in verse 27 closes that off, and it is the answer to the strawman that this framework has God sharing the act of creation.
entries.ur: Ch 3, God's Entourage; Ch 5, As in Heaven, So on Earth
sources: Heiser, “Monotheism, Polytheism, Monolatry, or Henotheism? Toward an Assessment of Divine Plurality in the Hebrew Bible,” BBR 18:1 (2008): 1-30
Heiser, “Monotheism and the Language of Divine Plurality in the Hebrew Bible and the Dead Sea Scrolls,” Tyndale Bulletin 65:1 (2014): 85-100
Unseen Realm chs. 3, 5

entries.title: Psalm 82
entries.summary: God stands in the divine assembly and passes sentence on the elohim He put in charge.
entries.plain: The real question: are “the gods” here actual spiritual beings under God's authority, or just a poetic name for human judges? **Animal** covers a whale and a mouse. It tells you what kind of thing something is, not how big or how important. Now imagine your only word for human also worked that way, so a king and a newborn got the same label, and rank had to come from somewhere else in the sentence. This card reads “the gods” as real, corrupt spiritual beings under God, not human judges.
entries.prob: Four moves in eight verses, and one reading has to carry all four. Verse 1 has God standing in an assembly of elohim. Verse 6 calls them sons of the Most High. Verse 7 sentences them to die like men. Verse 8 asks God to arise and inherit all the nations.
entries.res: Divine beings holding delegated authority over the nations, judged for misrule, accounts for every one. Verse 6 names what they are, verse 7 strips it, and verse 8 asks for the allotment itself to be revoked. That closing line is why this psalm is the hinge rather than one passage among many: it is a prayer that the arrangement in Deuteronomy 32:8-9 come to an end. The two passages are one argument read from opposite ends.
entries.cost: The psalm never says when the delegation happened or who received it. That has to come from Deuteronomy 32:8-9, the most textually contested verse in the index. The strongest card here leans on the shakiest one, and that dependency should be stated rather than buried.
entries.alt: The human-judges reading handles verse 7 neatly and cannot explain the assembly in verse 1, the title in verse 6, or why verse 8 asks God to inherit the nations. Critical scholarship raises a harder objection from the other side, that verse 1 sets El presiding while Yahweh stands among the gods, making them two deities. Heiser answered that one in print rather than around it. Neither alternative carries all four moves.
entries.phrase: Verse 6 reads bene elyon, sons of the Most High. The same construction runs through the council texts under different divine names: bene ha-elohim in Job 1:6 and 38:7, bene elim in Psalm 89:6, and the disputed bene elohim against bene yisrael in Deuteronomy 32:8. It is one phrase family, and the referent stays divine everywhere it appears except in the single verse where one witness reads Israel.
entries.kjv: God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.
entries.kjvRole: the King James keeps the hard reading
entries.kjvNote: Worth showing because it cuts against the expectation. The 1611 translators left the gods in place. A reader who assumes modern versions invented the divine council can be handed a King James and read it there.
entries.lew: Lewis lets Tash be real. A false god in Narnia is not an empty idol but an actual being with actual worshippers and an actual claim, which is closer to Psalm 82 than most catechisms get.
entries.ur: Ch 3, God's Entourage; Ch 4, God Alone

entries.title: 1 Kings 22:19-23
entries.summary: Micaiah reports seeing Yahweh enthroned with the host standing to His right and left.
entries.plain: The real question: is this an actual exchange between God and other beings, or just a dramatic way of narrating a decision God already made alone? **Picture a commander asking a room for volunteers, someone stepping forward with a plan, and the commander approving it before sending them out.** That's a conversation with genuine give and take, not one person narrating a decision to themselves. This card takes it as exactly that: a real council with deliberation to match.
entries.prob: A prophet describes God asking for volunteers and approving a plan He could have executed alone. The scene is hard to read as figurative when the plan is then carried out.
entries.res: A council with actual members, genuine deliberation, and delegated execution accounts for the question, the volunteer, and the outcome without treating the vision as decorative.
entries.cost: It raises the problem of a deceiving spirit operating with permission, which the passage states and does not soften.
sources: Mullen, “Divine Assembly,” Anchor Yale Bible Dictionary 2:215-216
Min Suc Kee, “The Heavenly Council and its Type-Scene,” JSOT 31:3 (2007): 259-273
Fleming, “The Divine Council as Type Scene in the Hebrew Bible,” PhD diss., SBTS, 1989

entries.title: Job 1:6-12
entries.summary: The sons of God present themselves and the satan comes among them.
entries.plain: The real question: is “the satan” here the devil's proper name, or a job title for a prosecuting role in God's court? **"The accountant" names a job. "Mr. Accountant" would sound odd,** because accountant is doing the work of a title there, not a name. A figure in an old story gets introduced with "the" in front of a role-word the same way. That marks an office, not a specific someone. He's holding a position, not wearing a name badge. This card reads “the satan” as an office, not a name.
entries.prob: There is a scheduled convening, an attendance report, and a figure who must ask permission before acting. None of that fits a freelance enemy of God.
entries.res: An office within an assembly explains the attendance, the permission, and the limits placed on him in the same stroke.
entries.cost: It does not tell you whether the office-holder here is the same figure later theology calls Satan, or a role that later thought grew into that figure. The text simply moves on, and Walton's own split between how he reads Job 1 and Genesis 6:2 shows working scholars don't agree how much continuity to assume.
entries.alt: Reading the figure as the later Satan of the New Testament has to explain why he reports in, why he asks, and why he obeys the boundary.
entries.not: **The satan is a title here, not a name.** The Hebrew carries the definite article, which a proper name cannot take.
entries.phrase: The sons of God here are bene ha-elohim, the same construction as Genesis 6:2 and the Qumran reading of Deuteronomy 32:8. Walton reads it as divine in this verse and not in Genesis 6, which is the split recorded below.
entries.kjv: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them.
entries.kjvRole: the rendering that made a title into a name
entries.kjvNote: The capital S does the damage. Four centuries of English readers have met a character here rather than an office.
entries.wal: Walton affirms the divine council here without hesitation, which is the interesting part. The same phrase he declines to read supernaturally in Genesis 6 he reads supernaturally in Job. Whether that is inconsistency or context-sensitivity is a fair argument to have.
entries.ur: Ch 3; Ch 8, Only God is Perfect
sources: Parker, “Sons of (The) God(s),” Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible, 2nd ed.
Cooke, “The Sons of (the) God(s),” ZAW 76 (1964): 22-47
Ellen White, Yahweh’s Council: Its Structure and Membership (FAT 2/65; Mohr-Siebeck, 2014)
Walton, Job (NIV Application Commentary): the dissent

entries.title: Psalm 89:5-7
entries.summary: Yahweh is feared in the council of the holy ones, and nothing in the skies compares to Him.
entries.plain: The real question: does “nothing compares to you” only work if there's something real in the room to compare against? **“Best goalkeeper in the world” only means something if other goalkeepers exist. Call yourself unmatched in an empty room and the word does no work.** The praise here runs on that same logic: actual rivals in the room, all of them outclassed. This card takes the “holy ones” as a real company of divine beings, not poetic flourish.
entries.prob: The psalm proves God's uniqueness by comparing Him to others. A comparison to nothing proves nothing.
entries.res: The company of divine beings makes the argument work as written. Incomparability among peers is a stronger claim than solitude.
entries.cost: The psalm never describes what the holy ones actually do beyond standing in the comparison. It does not tell you whether they have any agency of their own, the way the council does in Job or 1 Kings 22, or exist here purely as a rhetorical foil for God's uniqueness.
entries.phrase: Verse 6 reads bene elim, sons of the gods, a third variation on the same construction.
sources: Parker, “Sons of (The) God(s),” DDD 2nd ed.
Miller, “Cosmology and World Order in the Old Testament: The Divine Council as Cosmic-Political Symbol,” HBT 9:2 (1987): 53-78
Unseen Realm ch. 4 bibliography

entries.title: Isaiah 6:1-8
entries.summary: The throne room, the seraphim, and the plural question, who will go for us.
entries.plain: The real question: is this writer overhearing an actual conversation already in progress, or is “us” just a royal way of saying “me”? **Walk into a meeting already running and someone asks the room, “Who's going to take this one?” You don't have to ask who else is there. The question itself tells you the room isn't empty.** This vision reads the same way: a real council, mid-session, that Isaiah has just stepped into.
entries.prob: Who is the us. The question is addressed to someone, and Isaiah answers as though he has stepped into a conversation already running.
entries.res: A session in progress explains the plural, the cleansing before he may speak, and the fact that he volunteers rather than being commanded.
entries.cost: It never says who exactly the plural “us” includes, and it does not explain why a human being can volunteer for the kind of council errand that, in Job or 1 Kings 22, is carried out by non-human members only. Isaiah's own status in that room is left unaddressed.
entries.ur: Ch 31, Who Will Go For Us?
sources: Mullen, The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature (1980)
Min Suc Kee, JSOT 31:3 (2007): 259-273
Unseen Realm ch. 31

entries.title: Daniel 7:9-14
entries.summary: Thrones are set in place, plural, the court sits, and one like a son of man comes on the clouds.
entries.plain: The real question: who fills the other thrones, and does a second enthroned figure split God into two? **A courtroom has a judge's bench and a jury box. Seeing “thrones were set in place” (plural) with only one figure named is like walking in and finding the jury box built before anyone tells you who's sitting there.** The seats being there is the point, even before the names are given. This card reads the extra thrones as filled and the second enthroned figure as a real co-ruler, not a rival god.
entries.prob: Thrones is plural and the text never says who fills the others. A second figure then receives dominion that belongs to God alone.
entries.res: A seated court with a second enthroned figure accounts for the plural, the books, and the transfer of dominion without splitting God in two.
entries.cost: The identity of the other thrones is left open here and the index does not close it.
entries.stNote: The Parables develop this Son of Man into a pre-existent enthroned figure. Dating is disputed and no fragment of this section turned up at Qumran, so it carries less weight than the Watchers material.
entries.ur: Ch 29, The Rider of the Clouds
sources: Collins and Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia; Fortress, 1993)
Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch: A Commentary (Hermeneia; Fortress, 2001)
Unseen Realm ch. 29

entries.title: Isaiah 24:21-23
entries.summary: Yahweh punishes the host of heaven above and the kings of earth below, then reigns before His elders.
entries.plain: The real question: why does this text judge sky-powers and earthly kings in the very same breath, as if they were the same kind of problem? A report saying “the executives and the faulty machines both failed inspection” only makes sense if the machines were also somebody's job to maintain. **Judging “the host of heaven” and “the kings of the earth” together only makes sense if both were handed responsibility, and both failed at it.** This card reads it as one failure at two levels, sky-powers and kings alike.
entries.prob: Heavenly powers and earthly kings are judged in one sentence, as though they were the same kind of problem.
entries.res: Delegated rule that went wrong at both levels makes the pairing ordinary rather than poetic.
entries.cost: It does not identify which specific figures make up “the host of heaven” here, or say what their punishment actually consists of. The parallel with earthly kings works as an argument, but the passage stops short of naming names on either side.
sources: Willis, “Yahweh’s Elders (Isa 24, 23): Senior Officials of the Divine Court,” ZAW 103:3 (1991): 375-385
Unseen Realm ch. 20 bibliography

entries.title: Deuteronomy 32:8-9
entries.summary: The Most High divided the nations, and the number He divided them by is where the whole argument turns.
entries.plain: The real question: did God divide the nations by Israel's future headcount, or hand them over to a council of spiritual beings? **Two handwritten copies of the same letter from your grandmother, one older and torn, one newer and complete, and they do not say the same thing in one line.** Nobody forged anything. Somebody copied something. Which one do you read at the funeral, and how do you decide? This card leans on the older, shorter copies: divine beings, not a future headcount.
entries.prob: The nations are divided according to a number, and on the traditional reading that number is Israel, who does not exist yet. The verse is dating the division of humanity to a yardstick that will not be born for generations.
entries.res: Divine beings as the number fits the table of nations in Genesis 10, explains the contrast in verse 9 where Yahweh keeps Jacob for Himself, and supplies the background that Deuteronomy 4:19, Daniel 10 and Acts 17 all assume.
entries.cost: It requires preferring the Qumran and Septuagint witnesses over the Masoretic Text, and the Qumran evidence is fragmentary. Anyone who says this is settled is overselling it.
entries.alt: The Masoretic reading has to explain the chronology, and usually does so by appeal to the seventy of Jacob's household in Genesis 46, which indexes the division of all nations to a family not yet in existence. That is not impossible. It is a patch, and it is the only problem that reading solves.
entries.phrase: This is the one verse in the family where a witness reads Israel instead of a divine title. Everywhere else the construction is bene ha-elohim, bene elim or bene elyon and nobody disputes that the referent is divine. That asymmetry is itself an argument, and it is the reason the Qumran reading is taken seriously rather than dismissed.
entries.edit:
Name the words. 4QDeut-j (4Q37) reads bene elohim, sons of God. The Masoretic Text reads bene yisrael, sons of Israel. The Septuagint reads angels of God, with some copies reading sons of God. One phrase, three witnesses, and the Qumran scroll is roughly a thousand years older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscript.

The direction of the change is the argument. A scribe copying an innocuous phrase like sons of Israel has no reason to replace it with sons of God, which is theologically explosive. A scribe copying sons of God in a period anxious about polytheism has an obvious reason to do the reverse. Changes run from difficult toward safe, not the other way.

And it happens twice in the same song. Verse 43 has the same kind of minus in the same chapter, and the odds of two independent accidents both removing heavenly beings from one poem are what make the accidental-corruption explanation hard to hold.
entries.kjv: When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.
entries.kjvNote: Three witnesses, three readings: the Masoretic Text has sons of Israel, the Septuagint has angels of God, the Qumran scroll has sons of God. The King James follows the Masoretic and was not first to do so. Wycliffe in 1395, Tyndale, the Great Bible, Matthew's, the Bishops' and the Geneva all read children of Israel, and the NKJV, NASB, NIV and CSB still do. Nobody changed anything recently. Translators are choosing between witnesses that have always disagreed.
entries.stNote: The Dead Sea Scrolls witness is the reason this reading is arguable at all rather than a conjecture.
entries.lew: Seventeen years before Heiser was born, Lewis gave every planet its own Oyarsa and made Earth the one whose ruler went bent and was confined. Thulcandra, the silent planet, is this cosmic geography written as a novel. He arrived through medieval cosmology rather than Ugaritic and landed in the same place.
entries.ur: Ch 14, Divine Allotment; Ch 15, Cosmic Geography
sources: Lewis, Out of the Silent Planet (1938), in your books vault: the Oyarsa of Thulcandra “became bent,” was driven out of the heavens and “bound in the air of his own world”; the planet “alone is outside the heaven, and no message comes from it”

entries.title: Deuteronomy 32:43; Hebrews 1:6
entries.summary: The end of the Song of Moses, where the Masoretic text is one line and every other witness is longer.
entries.plain: The real question: did later copies of this song lose a line about angels worshiping God, or did earlier copies add one that was never there? **Imagine a will with six copies at six law offices. Five include a paragraph. The sixth (the one that became everyone's default) is missing it.** That's not proof the paragraph was added later; it could just as easily be the copy that lost something. This card takes the longer reading as original, and the shorter one as the copy that lost a line.
entries.prob: Hebrews 1:6 quotes a line about all God's angels worshipping the Son and presents it as Scripture. That line is not in the Hebrew text behind the King James or most English Old Testaments.
entries.res: If the longer text is original, Hebrews is quoting Deuteronomy as it stood in the first century, and the chapter lost divine beings at two points rather than one. That also explains why the Song of Moses ends on a cosmic note instead of a national one, which fits how it opened.
entries.cost: The witnesses agree against the Masoretic Text and do not agree with each other. 4QDeut-q calls on all the gods, the Septuagint on the angels of God in most copies and the sons of God in some. Reconstructing one original from three disagreeing witnesses is not the same as having it.
entries.alt: The strongest reply is that Hebrews 1:6 is quoting Psalm 97:7 rather than Deuteronomy 32:43, and that the sons of God reading in the Greek is a minority one with thin transmission. That reply is serious and it still has to accept that this chapter is shorter in the Masoretic Text than in every other witness at exactly the two places where divine beings would appear.
entries.edit:
The second minus in the same chapter, and the one that can be checked against a New Testament quotation. The Masoretic Text of verse 43 has a single line, rejoice O nations with his people. 4QDeut-q (4Q44) has a bicolon that adds a call for all the gods to bow down to him. The Septuagint has two bicola and includes the angels of God, with some copies reading sons of God. Justin Martyr quotes the longer Greek form in the second century, word for word as Hebrews has it.

So the pattern in Deuteronomy 32 is not one disputed word. It is heavenly beings absent from the Masoretic Text at verse 8 and again at verse 43, present in the Qumran material and the Greek at both, and quoted from the longer form inside the New Testament itself.
entries.kjv: Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people.
entries.kjvRole: the verse where the King James is the shorter one
entries.kjvNote: The 1611 translators followed the Hebrew they had, faithfully. The result is that the words Hebrews 1:6 quotes as Scripture are not present in their Deuteronomy. That is the mirror image of the usual argument about verses missing from modern Bibles, running in the opposite direction, and it is the one almost nobody raises.
entries.stNote: Preserves the longer ending of the Song with the call to the gods. Together with 4QDeut-j at verse 8, it is the reason this chapter is the most text-critically important in Deuteronomy.
entries.ur: Ch 14, Divine Allotment; Ch 15, Cosmic Geography
sources: 4QDeut-q (4Q44), Qumran
Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 269
Heiser, Bibliotheca Sacra 158 (2001): 52-74
Justin Martyr, quoting the longer Greek form in the second century
The Masoretic-priority reply, that Hebrews 1:6 cites Psalm 97:7: the counter-case, still to be pulled to a named source

entries.title: Deuteronomy 4:19-20
entries.summary: Israel must not worship the host of heaven, which Yahweh allotted to all the other peoples.
entries.plain: The real question: if God really handed the sky-powers to the other nations, why is it wrong for Israel to worship them too? A parent gives each kid their own chore and their own allowance: one kid can't then claim a sibling's allowance too, even though the money is just as real either way. **What was handed to someone else stays off limits to you, precisely because it was never yours to begin with.** This card reads the sky-powers as real, delegated rulers over the nations, not just stars.
entries.prob: God is said to have assigned the host of heaven to the nations, and then forbids Israel the same thing. An assignment is not a prohibition, so what was given to them.
entries.res: Delegated authority over the nations makes the sentence read straight. What Israel may not do is worship what the others were placed under.
entries.cost: Nothing here explains why God would make such an arrangement, and Deuteronomy does not say.
entries.alt: Readings that treat the host of heaven as mere astronomy have to explain in what sense stars were allotted to peoples as an act of God rather than simply existing over everyone.
sources: Lewis, The Discarded Image (1964)
Heiser, “Does Deuteronomy 32:17 Assume or Deny the Reality of Other Gods?” Bible Translator 59:3 (2008): 137-145
Zatelli, “Astrology and the Worship of the Stars in the Bible,” ZAW 103:1 (1991): 86-99
Lelli, “Stars,” DDD 2nd ed.
Unseen Realm ch. 15

entries.title: Genesis 11:1-9
entries.summary: Babel, the scattering, and the moment the nations are set aside.
entries.plain: The real question: why does one tower-building project end with the founding of every nation on earth? Isn't that wildly out of proportion? **Grounding one kid for breaking curfew and then reorganizing the entire household's chore chart is a strange response, unless the reorganizing was the actual point and the grounding was only the occasion for it.** This story reads the same way once you notice how much bigger the outcome is than the offense. This card reads Babel as the moment the nations were handed off, not a fable about language.
entries.prob: The punishment for building a tower is the creation of the nations, which reads as disproportionate unless something else is happening.
entries.res: Read as the disinheritance behind Deuteronomy 32, Babel produces the map that the rest of the Old Testament assumes, and Pentecost becomes its answer rather than a coincidence.
entries.cost: Genesis itself never mentions divine beings here. The connection is made by Deuteronomy, not by the Babel account.
sources: van der Toorn, “Nimrod Before and After the Bible,” HTR 83:1 (1990): 1-29
Sarna, Genesis (JPS Torah Commentary, 1989)
Unseen Realm ch. 14 bibliography

entries.title: Daniel 10:13, 20-21
entries.summary: A prince of Persia resists for twenty-one days, a prince of Greece is coming, and Michael fights for Israel.
entries.plain: The real question: what could possibly hold up a heavenly messenger for three weeks, if the only players are God and humans? A diplomat can be delayed for weeks by a hostile foreign office: not because the office is physically stronger, but because it has real jurisdiction there. **A messenger stopped for twenty-one days by something called “the prince of Persia” reads like exactly that kind of territorial standoff, not an empty hallway with nothing in it.** This card reads the “princes” as real territorial powers, not human kings.
entries.prob: A messenger from God is delayed three weeks by something called the prince of Persia, and needs help to get through. Nothing in a flat angelology explains a delay.
entries.res: Territorial powers with actual jurisdiction account for the delay, the naming by nation, and Michael's specific attachment to Israel.
entries.cost: It does not explain the mechanics of how a territorial power could hold up a heavenly messenger for a fixed number of days, and the reading depends on “prince” meaning the same non-human thing in verses 13 and 20 as it clearly does for Michael in verse 21. The text itself never states outright that the Persian and Greek princes aren't human rulers.
entries.alt: Readings that treat the princes as human kings have to explain how a human detains a heavenly messenger for twenty-one days.
entries.lew: The siege of Thulcandra is the same idea in fiction: a planet under a hostile ruler, quarantined, with the loyal powers held at the boundary and the war conducted across it.
entries.lewSrc: Out of the Silent Planet; That Hideous Strength
sources: Lewis, Out of the Silent Planet and Perelandra, in your books vault: “the phase of the great siege, the phase which gave to our planet its name of Thulcandra, the silent planet”
Clifford, “History and Myth in Daniel 10-12,” BASOR (1975): 23-26
Collins and Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia; Fortress, 1993)
Ronn Johnson, “The Old Testament Background for Paul’s Principalities and Powers,” PhD diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 2004
Unseen Realm ch. 15 bibliography

entries.title: Acts 17:26-27
entries.summary: Paul tells the Areopagus that God fixed the times and the boundaries of the nations.
entries.plain: The real question: is Paul just describing ordinary history, or is he announcing that an actual, standing arrangement over the nations is being cancelled? **Announcing “the old lease is up” only lands as news if there really was a lease.** Paul tells a pagan crowd that God fixed the nations' boundaries, then pivots straight into an announcement. That only makes sense as news if the boundaries were the real thing, not just a figure of speech. This card reads Paul as announcing the end of that arrangement, not narrating history.
entries.prob: Paul chooses allotment language in front of a pagan audience and then announces that the arrangement is ending.
entries.res: If the boundaries were an actual assignment, the sermon is an announcement that the assignment is being revoked, which is why he goes straight to the resurrection.
entries.cost: The verse can be read as ordinary providence over history, and on its own it does not force the stronger reading.
sources: Ronn Johnson, PhD diss., DTS, 2004
Arnold, “Returning to the Domain of the Powers: Stoicheia as Evil Spirits in Galatians 4:3, 9,” NovT 38:1 (1996): 55-76
Unseen Realm chs. 15, 32

entries.title: Genesis 3:1-15
entries.summary: The nachash in the garden, and the sentence passed on it.
entries.plain: The real question: is the speaking creature in the garden just an animal, or something else operating there with real authority? **A courtroom doesn't sentence a stray dog the way it sentences a person: the severity of a sentence tells you what kind of defendant is standing there.** The sentence this creature receives reads like it was written for someone who knew exactly what they were doing, not an animal that wandered in. This card reads the serpent as a real, rebellious spiritual being, not a literal snake.
entries.prob: A creature inside sacred space speaks, knows what God said, and is sentenced in language that outruns anything you could say to an animal.
entries.res: A divine rebel operating in Eden accounts for the access, the knowledge, the authority in the conversation, and the scope of the curse.
entries.cost: Genesis never names him, and every identification after this point is supplied from elsewhere in the canon.
entries.lew: Lewis wrote the temptation again on an unfallen world and gave the tempter a borrowed body. The Un-man argues well, never tires, and wears down by persistence rather than cleverness, which is a sharper reading of the scene than most commentaries manage.
sources: Lewis, Perelandra (1943), in your books vault: the Un-man

entries.title: Ezekiel 28:11-19
entries.summary: A guardian cherub in Eden, on the holy mountain, cast out for pride.
entries.plain: The real question: is this really about Satan's fall from heaven, or a human king mocked with borrowed, older imagery? **A political cartoon draws a stubborn official as a mule, ears and all.** Nobody thinks he actually has hooves. The artist borrowed a shape everyone already recognizes to land one point. A writer aimed a poem at a real king the same way, dressing him in older, half-remembered imagery about a magnificent guardian's fall. The costume is the insult. This card reads the passage as borrowed cosmic imagery aimed at a human king, not Satan's biography.
entries.prob: The oracle is addressed to the king of Tyre and then describes him in Eden, on the mountain of God, as an anointed cherub. The description overshoots the addressee.
entries.res: A known cosmic rebel story used as the template for a taunt against a king explains both layers without making either one disappear.
entries.cost: It does not tell you the passage is about Satan, and the reading is regularly used to smuggle that conclusion back in. The index files it contested for that reason.
entries.alt: A strictly human reading has to account for Eden, the holy mountain and the cherub. A strictly satanic reading has to account for the fact that the oracle names a king and is written as a lament over him.
entries.not: **Not a resume for Satan.** The worship-leader claim has a traceable source, and it is a translation choice rather than anything in the Hebrew.
entries.kjv: the workmanship of thy tabrets and of thy pipes was prepared in thee in the day that thou wast created.
entries.kjvNote: That clause is the entire basis of the claim that Satan was heaven's worship leader. Older commentators reading the same King James took the tabrets and pipes as the court music of a Tyrian king at his coronation. Modern versions render the line as settings and mountings of jewelry, and the Hebrew word behind pipes appears nowhere else, which is why the verse is argued rather than settled.
sources: Page, “The Astral Revolt,” PhD diss., Harvard, 1990
Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible, 275-278 (El)

entries.title: Isaiah 14:12-15
entries.summary: Helel ben-shachar, shining one, son of the dawn, falls from heaven.
entries.plain: The real question: is “Lucifer” a name for Satan, or a title mocking a human king with borrowed legend? Call someone **"the guy who flew too close to the sun"** and everyone hears the insult, no myth lecture needed: the doomed-flight story does the work by itself. An old poem mocks a real king the same way, dressing him as a legendary figure who tried to rule the sky and fell. The costume carries the insult, not a biography. Same move as the Ezekiel taunt: a human king in borrowed legend, not Satan's origin story.
entries.prob: A taunt song against the king of Babylon suddenly describes someone trying to set a throne above the stars of God, then verse 16 has onlookers staring at a man.
entries.res: A cosmic rebel motif borrowed to mock a human king holds both halves at once, which is exactly what the genre of a mashal does.
entries.cost: It leaves the origin of the motif outside the Bible, in Canaanite material, which some readers will find a cost in itself.
entries.alt: Reading the passage as a straight biography of Satan has to explain verse 16 and the funeral-dirge form. Reading it as purely human has to explain the throne above the stars.
entries.not: **Lucifer is not a name here.** It is Latin for the morning star, carried into English from the Vulgate.
entries.kjv: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!
entries.kjvNote: The proper noun enters English right here. Jerome rendered helel as lucifer, a common Latin noun for the morning star, and the King James carried it across untranslated and capitalized. Most of what people think they know about Satan's fall runs through this one word.

entries.title: Genesis 6:1-4
entries.summary: The sons of God take wives, and the Nephilim are in the earth.
entries.plain: The real question: were the “sons of God” who married human women fallen spiritual beings, or just powerful human rulers? Someone tells the neighbourhood story about the founding family, all heroism and destiny. **You tell the same events back with the same names and every detail intact, and in your version they come off badly.** You have not invented anything. You have retold their story against them. This card reads the “sons of God” as real spiritual beings, retelling an old story as an indictment.
entries.prob: Four verses interrupt a genealogy, introduce a category of being, produce offspring the text calls mighty men of renown, and then the flood arrives. The passage is doing work in the narrative and a flat reading leaves it doing none.
entries.res: The supernatural reading is the one that pays across the whole canon rather than in one place. It explains the interruption, the Nephilim, the giant clans in Numbers and Joshua, the conquest rationale, Jude and 2 Peter, the demonology the Gospels assume, and the unanimous Second Temple understanding. No other reading reaches more than two of those.
entries.cost: It does not explain how Nephilim appear after the flood. Heiser answers with a second incursion, and that is a patch. It should be named as one rather than folded in quietly.
entries.alt: The Sethite view solves a biological discomfort and leaves the Nephilim, the giant clans, the Second Temple consensus, Jude and Peter unexplained. Walton's royalty reading handles the ANE parallel well and still has to account for what Jude and Peter thought they were talking about.
entries.not: **Not aliens, not Anunnaki, not a lost civilization.** Sequence also matters: pagan mythology did not descend from the Nephilim, the polemic runs the other way.
entries.phrase: Bene ha-elohim again, identical to Job 1:6, where nobody argues the referent is human. Any reading that makes the phrase human here has to explain why the same words mean something else two books later.
entries.kjv: There were giants in the earth in those days.
entries.kjvRole: the rendering that shaped the tradition
entries.kjvNote: The King James translates rather than transliterates, following the Septuagint's gigantes. That choice is why the English-speaking world says giants and not Nephilim, and it quietly takes a side in the etymology argument.
entries.stNote: Shemihazah leads the oath, Asael teaches metallurgy and cosmetics. Jubilees 5 and the Genesis Apocryphon read the passage the same way. Whatever a modern reader thinks, this is how Second Temple Jews read it.
entries.wal: Walton does not ignore the Mesopotamian evidence, he reads it the other way. In The Genesis Debate he argues the sons of God are royalty, ANE kings claiming divine descent, on the Gilgamesh parallel, with three objections to the divine reading: no obvious connection to the purposes of Genesis, awkward placement in a sequence otherwise tracking human sin, and a mythological tone at odds with the world as we know it. In the NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible he works the same apkallu material Heiser uses, but identifies the Nephilim themselves with the sages rather than with their offspring. The honest part is what he concedes there: on that reading the term Nephilim remains unexplained, and so does its connection to the inhabitants of the land in Numbers 13:33. Two scholars, one body of cuneiform evidence, opposite conclusions, and each naming what his own reading leaves open.

entries.title: Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4
entries.summary: Angels who abandoned their proper dwelling, held in chains until judgment.
entries.plain: The real question: what specific, well-known story are these two writers assuming their readers already know, without ever spelling it out? **Someone at a family gathering says, “well, you remember what happened at Thanksgiving,” and everyone nods. The story never gets retold because the whole room already owns it.** These two writers mention an angelic rebellion the same way: assumed, not narrated. This card reads that assumed story as Genesis 6, read the way the first century read it.
entries.prob: Two writers refer to an angelic sin as something their readers already know, and never explain it. The reference assumes a story.
entries.res: Genesis 6 as read in the Second Temple period supplies the story both writers assume, which is why neither felt the need to narrate it.
entries.cost: Neither text names Genesis 6 outright, so the identification is an inference from proximity and vocabulary.
entries.alt: Readings that decline the Genesis 6 link have to supply some other widely known angelic sin that first century readers would have recognized without explanation, and none is on offer.
entries.stNote: The binding, the place of imprisonment, and the refused intercession are all in the Watchers material. Peter and Jude are not inventing the imagery.
entries.wal: Walton's reply is that Jude's word for the sin is sexual immorality generally and that 2 Peter never names which sin the angels committed, so neither text pins Genesis 6 as tightly as the supernatural reading needs.

post.title: Who Wrote the Book of Jude?

entries.title: Jude 14-15
entries.summary: Jude quotes Enoch, the seventh from Adam, by name.
entries.plain: The real question: does quoting a book by name as prophecy mean the writer considered that whole book equally authoritative? A speaker can quote one line from a well-known poem, name the poet, and call the line true, without thereby declaring the poet's entire body of work equally authoritative. **Quoting one line and naming its source is not the same act as officially canonizing everything that source ever wrote.** This card reads the quotation as evidence of what the first century actually read, not an endorsement of a whole book.
entries.prob: A canonical letter quotes a non-canonical book as prophecy, by name, without apology.
entries.res: Taking it as evidence of what the first century read, rather than as a problem to be managed, explains the quotation and the surrounding argument at once.
entries.cost: It does not settle what Jude thought about the book's authority, and nobody can.
entries.not: **Quotation is not canonization.** Paul quotes pagan poets too. Reversing Hermon's appendix walks the ancient debate rather than settling it by assertion.
entries.stNote: The quoted line sits in the opening oracle of the Book of the Watchers.
entries.rh: Appendix, the ancient debate on the inspiration of 1 Enoch

entries.title: Numbers 13:33
entries.summary: The spies report the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, and call themselves grasshoppers.
entries.plain: The real question: were there really still giant clans in the land, or are these just scared scouts exaggerating? **A news story can quote an eyewitness by name and still say, a paragraph later, that the account was exaggerated.** Quoting someone isn't the same as endorsing them: the story reports the claim, it doesn't confirm it. An old account does exactly this: it records what a group of scouts said, then flatly calls their report a bad one. This card still takes the giant clans as continuous with Genesis 6, even inside an unreliable report.
entries.prob: A word from before the flood turns up in a reconnaissance report centuries after it, in a land Israel is about to enter.
entries.res: Continuity between Genesis 6 and the giant clans gives the conquest a rationale that is theological rather than ethnic, and explains why particular regions get particular language.
entries.cost: The line sits inside a report the narrative goes on to call a bad report, so its reliability is questioned by the text itself.
entries.alt: Reading Nephilim here as rhetorical exaggeration is available and leaves open why the narrator keeps tracking these clans by name through Deuteronomy, Joshua and Samuel.
entries.kjv: And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants.
entries.kjvRole: the rendering that shaped the tradition
entries.kjvNote: Same translation choice as Genesis 6:4. In Hebrew a reader sees Nephilim in both places and draws the same line, so the connection survives the translation question either way.
entries.stRef: The Book of Giants, 4Q203 and related fragments
entries.stNote: A Qumran text about the giants and their fate, closely tied to the Enochic Watchers tradition.
entries.wal: Walton grants the giants nothing load-bearing. In his reading herem removes a community identity rather than exterminating a bloodline, and the Canaanites are not being punished for sin at all. That removes the need for a Nephilim rationale, which is the exact need Heiser's reading exists to meet.

entries.title: Joshua 11:21-22
entries.summary: Joshua cuts off the Anakim from the hill country, and none are left except in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.
entries.plain: The real question: why does one specific group get its own separate wrap-up, naming exactly where its survivors ended up? A report on a completed evacuation that adds “except for a few families who relocated to three named towns” is setting something up for later: that kind of specificity is a promise, not filler. **Naming exactly where the last of the Anakim went reads the same way: a loose thread, left for later.** This card reads that loose thread as pointing straight at Goliath.
entries.prob: The narrator gives the Anakim their own summary statement, separate from the general conquest account, and then names exactly where survivors remain.
entries.res: A targeted objective explains the separate summary and sets up Goliath of Gath without anyone having to reach for it later.
entries.cost: The chapter never says why the Anakim rate their own paragraph. The reason is imported from Numbers 13.
entries.wal: Walton reads the conquest account as recapitulating order over chaos rather than as a campaign against a bloodline, and takes the destruction language as ordinary ancient war rhetoric. Two coherent readings of the same chapter, and the difference is method, not piety.

entries.title: Leviticus 16:8-10
entries.summary: One goat for Yahweh, one goat for Azazel, sent into the wilderness.
entries.plain: The real question: is Azazel a place the goat gets sent to, or a being the goat gets sent away from? **One ticket for Dave, the other ticket for the bin.** That sentence is lopsided and your ear catches it. **One ticket for Dave, the other for Susan** is not. When a sentence sets up two slots the same way, both slots normally hold the same kind of thing. This card reads Azazel as a being, not a place, to keep that parallel intact.
entries.prob: The verse builds a parallel, one lot for the LORD and one lot for Azazel. If Azazel is a place, the parallel is between a person and a location, which is not how the sentence is built.
entries.res: Azazel as a named being keeps the grammatical parallel intact and connects the wilderness destination to the place where the Second Temple material says the rebel was bound.
entries.cost: Nothing in Leviticus identifies Azazel as anything. The identification is entirely imported, and the index files this contested for that reason alone.
entries.alt: The destination reading keeps the theology tidy and breaks the parallel. The scapegoat reading avoids the question by inventing an English word for it.
entries.not: **Not a sacrifice to a demon.** Nothing is offered to Azazel. The goat carries sin out to the place where the rebel belongs.
entries.kjv: one lot for the LORD, and the other lot for the scapegoat.
entries.kjvRole: the rendering that hid the question
entries.kjvNote: Scapegoat is a coined English word, built to make azazel mean the goat that goes away. It reads smoothly and removes the problem, because the reader is never told there is a proper noun in the Hebrew.
entries.stNote: Asael is bound and cast into the desert at Dudael. The wilderness location is the link that makes the Leviticus reading more than a hunch.
entries.ur: Ch 24, The Place of the Serpent

entries.title: Mark 5:1-20
entries.summary: Legion, in Gentile territory east of the lake, begging not to be sent to the abyss.
entries.plain: The real question: why do the demons in this story beg for a temporary home in pigs instead of the place they clearly already know about and dread? **Someone begging for a bunk instead of being sent back to one specific address only makes sense if that address is real, and they know exactly what's waiting there.** These spirits negotiate like prisoners avoiding a real transfer, not vague evil in the abstract. This card reads that address as the same confinement described in the Second Temple Watchers material.
entries.prob: The demons want a body badly enough to ask for pigs, and they know there is a specific place they can be sent instead.
entries.res: A demonology in which these spirits are disembodied and awaiting confinement explains both the request and the dread, and explains why the scene is staged outside Israel.
entries.cost: Mark never explains where demons come from, and the explanation used here comes from outside the canon.
entries.stNote: The evil spirits that trouble the earth are the disembodied spirits of the dead giants. That is where Second Temple Judaism got its demonology, and it explains why demons in the Gospels want bodies.

entries.title: 1 Samuel 28:13
entries.summary: The medium at Endor sees an elohim coming up out of the earth, and it is Samuel.
entries.plain: The real question: did the medium actually see a god, or does the word just mean “someone from the realm of the dead”? **Category words don't rank things: "vehicle" covers a skateboard and a jet, with no claim about which matters more.** Imagine your only word for a dead person worked as a category too, usable the instant someone was gone, without claiming anything about their importance. An old story uses that kind of word for someone who just died, naming the category, not the rank. This card reads “a god” the same way: a real category word, not a claim about status.
entries.prob: A dead prophet is called elohim. If the word means deity by rank, the sentence is impossible.
entries.res: Elohim as a term marking which realm a being inhabits rather than its rank lets this verse, Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32 all use the word consistently.
entries.cost: It requires accepting that the narrative treats the appearance as genuinely Samuel, which some readers will not grant.
entries.phrase: Not the sons-of-X construction, but the same lexical argument. If elohim marks the realm a being inhabits rather than its rank, this verse and Psalm 82:1 use the word the same way.
entries.kjv: I saw gods ascending out of the earth.
entries.kjvRole: the rendering that kept the question visible
entries.kjvNote: The King James keeps gods, plural, which preserves the oddity. Versions rendering it a divine being or a spirit smooth the sentence and remove the evidence that elohim is a category term.
sources: Heiser, “Should אלהים with Plural Predication be Translated ‘Gods’?” Bible Translator 61:3 (2010): 123-136

entries.title: John 10:31-36
entries.summary: Jesus answers a charge of blasphemy by quoting Psalm 82.
entries.plain: The real question: why does quoting one old psalm about “gods” work as a legal defense against a charge of blasphemy? **Quoting one line from an old court ruling only defuses an accusation if the judge already knows that ruling and accepts it as binding.** Say it to someone unfamiliar with the case and it lands as nothing. A speaker facing a serious accusation here reaches for one old, short line, and it works: that only makes sense if the room already recognized it as authoritative. This card reads that recognition as proof a real divine-council reading was common ground at the time.
entries.prob: Under a charge that carries the death penalty, Jesus reaches for an obscure psalm about gods. The defense only works if his accusers already understood it.
entries.res: A live divine council framework in the first century explains why the quotation functions as a defense at all.
entries.cost: The text shows the accusers drop the stoning attempt, not that they agreed with the argument. Silence isn't the same as concession, and John immediately has them try to seize Jesus anyway two verses later, which this defense doesn't obviously prevent.
entries.not: **Not Jesus claiming to be merely a god.** The Greek construction in verse 33 appears elsewhere referring specifically to God the Father.
sources: Heiser, “You’ve Seen One Elohim, You’ve Seen Them All? A Critique of Mormonism’s Use of Psalm 82,” FARMS Review 19:1 (2007): 221-266

entries.title: Matthew 1:1-6
entries.summary: Four women named in the genealogy of Jesus, each with an irregular story.
entries.plain: The real question: why does a genealogy that normally lists only men suddenly name four women, each with an irregular story attached? **A family tree that skips every in-law except four, and all four carry some kind of scandal, is not an accident: someone chose to include them, and chose them as a matched set.** The question is what that set is pointing back to. This card reads it as a deliberate echo of the Genesis 6 pattern.
entries.prob: Genealogies of this kind do not usually name women. These four are named and the obvious candidates are not.
entries.res: Heiser proposes the four would have called the Genesis 6 pattern to mind for a first century reader.
entries.cost: The argument runs on association and nothing in Matthew states it. This is a proposal, not a result, and the card says so.
entries.alt: The common explanations, that all four were Gentiles or all four were scandalous, each fail on at least one of the four. That is why the question stays open rather than why this answer wins.
entries.rh: Ch 5, The Sin of the Watchers and the Genealogy of Jesus

entries.title: Matthew 16:13-20
entries.summary: Caesarea Philippi, the gates of Hades, and the confession.
entries.plain: The real question: why does the writer bother naming the exact location for this exchange, and what does that location have to do with talk of “gates”? **A story that specifies “he said it standing on the courthouse steps” wants you to notice the courthouse: the location is doing work the plain words alone don't do.** This spot is named on purpose, right before Jesus starts talking about gates that will not hold. This card reads the location as deliberate: a real site tied to the underworld in local belief.
entries.prob: Matthew tells us where this happened, which he rarely bothers to do, and the saying that follows is about gates.
entries.res: The location is doing work. Jesus asks at the foot of Hermon, in front of a cave locals treated as an entrance to the underworld, then names gates that will not hold.
entries.cost: Matthew does not comment on the setting, so the connection rests on geography and the reader's willingness to think the detail was deliberate.
sources: G. del Olmo Lete, “Bashan,” DDD 2nd ed., 161-163
Unseen Realm ch. 34; Reversing Hermon ch. 6
Vault: Reversing-Hermon-Reading-Guide-v2

entries.title: Matthew 17:1-8
entries.summary: The transfiguration, six days later, on a high mountain.
entries.plain: The real question: does it matter which mountain this is, or is “a high mountain” just scenery? **A story that says “they drove to a house” right after three pages at one specific address is quietly still talking about that same house.** This mountain scene follows immediately after one tied to a very particular place, where location was already doing real work. This card reads the unnamed mountain as Hermon, reclaiming the site of the Watchers' oath.
entries.prob: The mountain is unnamed, the timing is marked precisely, and the location follows immediately from Caesarea Philippi.
entries.res: Hermon as the mountain turns the scene into a reclaiming of the place where the Watchers swore their oath, which is where Reversing Hermon gets its title.
entries.cost: Matthew does not name the mountain, and a long tradition places the transfiguration at Tabor instead. This reading is stronger on geography than on evidence.
entries.stNote: The Watchers descend on the summit of Hermon and bind themselves by oath there. The mountain is named in the source, which is what makes the geography argument possible at all.
sources: 4QEn-a, the Aramaic Qumran fragment: the Mount Hermon reference is corrupt in the Ethiopic text of 1 Enoch 6:6 and its authenticity rests on this fragment and some Greek manuscripts. The geography argument stands or falls here.
G. del Olmo Lete, “Bashan,” Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible, 2nd ed., 161-163
Reversing Hermon ch. 6, notes 53, 161-162, 170
Vault: Reversing-Hermon-Reading-Guide-v2, 1 Enoch VI–XI mapping

entries.title: Luke 10:1-20
entries.summary: Seventy sent out, and Satan falling like lightning when they return.
entries.plain: The real question: why does a specific head-count and a comment about a cosmic fall show up back to back, as if they're one report and not two? **A manager sending exactly the right number of reps to cover every territory on the map, then getting a call that the old regional boss just got fired, is one story, not two unrelated updates.** The number and the falling-star line read like a single status report. This card reads the two halves as one announcement about the nations' allotment.
entries.prob: The number is specified and then Jesus responds to a report about demons with a statement about a fall from heaven. The two halves want a connection.
entries.res: A mission sized to the nations of Genesis 10 makes the number meaningful and makes the reply a status report on the allotment rather than a change of subject.
entries.cost: Luke never connects the number to the table of nations, and the manuscripts split seventy and seventy-two.
entries.kjv: After these things the Lord appointed other seventy also.
entries.kjvNote: The King James reads seventy. Several modern versions read seventy-two on manuscript grounds. The table of nations splits the same way, seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Septuagint, which is either a coincidence or the point.
sources: Ronn Johnson, PhD diss., DTS, 2004
Unseen Realm ch. 32; Reversing Hermon ch. 6
Manuscript evidence for seventy against seventy-two: not yet pulled to a named source

entries.title: Ephesians 6:10-12
entries.summary: The struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities, and cosmic powers.
entries.plain: The real question: what is this list of “rulers, authorities, cosmic powers” actually naming, and why does the writer never stop to explain any of it? **A memo that says “route this past Legal, Compliance, and the Regional Director” assumes you already know the org chart: the writer isn't inventing categories, just naming positions everyone in the building already recognizes.** This list works the same way: ordinary vocabulary to the writer, foreign to us. This card reads it as a real chain of command that rebelled, not rhetorical flourish.
entries.prob: Paul names four categories of hostile authority and places them in the heavenly realms, as though the reader already knows the org chart.
entries.res: A structure of delegated rule that rebelled makes the categories ordinary vocabulary rather than rhetorical flourish, and explains why Paul can list them without defining them.
entries.cost: Paul never says when or how this chain of command rebelled, and never maps “rulers,” “authorities,” or “cosmic powers” onto any specific figure named elsewhere in the canon. The org chart is real to him, but he leaves it completely unlabeled for anyone reading after the fact.
entries.lew: Lewis opened Screwtape by naming the two errors, disbelieving in devils and taking an excessive interest in them, then wrote a bureaucracy with ranks, reports and quotas. Treating the powers as organized without becoming lurid is exactly the discipline this index is trying to keep.
sources: Lewis, The Screwtape Letters (1942), in your books vault
Ronn Johnson, “The Old Testament Background for Paul’s Principalities and Powers,” PhD diss., DTS, 2004
Arnold, “Returning to the Domain of the Powers,” NovT 38:1 (1996): 55-76
Unseen Realm ch. 37

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 11:10
entries.summary: A woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels.
entries.plain: The real question: what do angels have to do with head coverings? What is Paul assuming his readers already know? **"Obviously, because of the Petersons, knock before entering."** If you weren't there for that incident, the reason makes no sense: the writer assumes a shared story never retold. One line in an old letter works the same way: the reason survives, the background everyone in the room already knew does not. This card reads the missing background as the Watchers story Paul's readers already knew.
entries.prob: The clause because of the angels has no antecedent anywhere in the letter and no obvious relevance to head covering.
entries.res: If Paul assumes the Watchers story, the clause has a referent and the instruction has a reason.
entries.cost: It still does not explain why head covering in particular is the response, and the index leaves that open.
entries.alt: Every competing reading either ignores the clause entirely or turns the angels into human messengers, which has no support in Paul's usage. Ignoring a clause is not solving it.
entries.kjv: For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.
entries.kjvRole: where the King James is more literal
entries.kjvNote: Power is the plain rendering of exousia, and it is what Paul wrote. Versions that render it a symbol of authority have supplied an interpretation in the text rather than leaving it for the reader.
entries.stNote: The descent narrative is the only background that makes an angelic audience relevant to what a woman has on her head.
entries.rh: Ch 8, the Head Covering of 1 Corinthians 11

entries.title: 1 Peter 3:18-22
entries.summary: Christ proclaims to the spirits in prison, the ones disobedient in the days of Noah.
entries.plain: The real question: why does the writer date this group's disobedience to one specific, ancient moment, instead of just saying “sinful people” in general? **Dating a group to one exact, ancient event, instead of describing them in general terms, is how you'd refer to a specific incident everyone already had a name for, not a vague category.** These “spirits in prison” are pinned to the days of Noah with exactly that kind of precision. This card reads them as those same imprisoned rebels from Genesis 6.
entries.prob: Peter dates the disobedience of the spirits to the days of Noah, which is a strange way to identify human souls and a precise way to identify something else.
entries.res: Imprisoned rebels from Genesis 6 explain the dating, the prison, and why a proclamation rather than an offer.
entries.cost: The passage is among the hardest in the New Testament and this reading does not make the baptism argument in verse 21 any easier.
entries.alt: The reading that takes the spirits as human dead has to explain the dating clause, and usually does not.
entries.not: **Not a harrowing-of-hell prooftext for human souls.** The spirits are identified by when they disobeyed.
entries.stNote: Enoch is sent to the imprisoned Watchers with a verdict and they get no reprieve. Peter has a figure making the same trip with a different message.
entries.rh: Ch 9, the Sin of the Watchers and Baptism
